channel.description: Recent content in history on Japan Specialty Traveler

item.title: Chiran: Peace Museum & Samurai Town — Guide
item.description: Chiran, a small town south of Kagoshima city, holds two very different but deeply memorable sights. The first is the Chiran Peace Museum for Kamikaze Pilots, a sobering and moving memorial on the site of a former WWII airbase from which many young ‘special attack’ (kamikaze) pilots flew on their final missions. Through their photographs, personal effects and heartbreaking farewell letters home, the museum conveys the human tragedy of war and stands as a powerful plea for peace.

item.title: Dejima Dutch Trading Post — Guide
item.description: Dejima, a small fan-shaped artificial island in Nagasaki, was for more than two centuries Japan’s sole point of contact with the Western world. During the Edo period, when Japan closed itself to foreigners under the sakoku isolation policy, the Dutch East India Company was confined to this tiny island, making it the country’s only window onto Western trade, science and culture — knowledge that flowed into Japan as ‘Dutch learning’ (rangaku).

item.title: Glover Garden — Guide
item.description: Glover Garden, on a hill in the Minamiyamate district overlooking Nagasaki harbour, is an open-air museum of Western-style residences built by the foreign merchants who settled here after Japan opened to the world in the mid-nineteenth century. Its centrepiece is the former home of Scottish trader Thomas Glover — the oldest Western-style wooden house in Japan — a graceful bungalow whose owner played a key role in Japan’s rapid modernisation, from shipbuilding to industry.

item.title: Goryokaku Fort & Tower — Guide
item.description: Goryokaku, in Hakodate in southern Hokkaido, is one of Japan’s most distinctive historical sites: a large, star-shaped Western-style fortress completed in 1866 near the end of the samurai era. Built to defend against foreign powers and later the site of a decisive battle of the Boshin War, its unusual five-pointed geometric design — inspired by European star forts — was intended to eliminate blind spots for defenders. Today the fort is a beautiful public park, its moats and earthen ramparts enclosing gardens, walking paths and the reconstructed Hakodate Magistrate’s Office.

item.title: Gunkei Temple, Hitoyoshi — Guide
item.description: In the castle town of Hitoyoshi, deep in the mountains of southern Kumamoto along the Kuma River, Gunkei Temple offers a quiet and historic stop amid the valley’s rich cultural heritage. Hitoyoshi flourished for centuries as the seat of the Sagara clan, who ruled the isolated Kuma region for some 700 years, and the town preserves an unusual concentration of old temples, shrines and cultural sites — including nationally important treasures — reflecting a distinctive local Buddhist and Shinto culture.

item.title: Hiroshima Castle: The Rebuilt Carp Castle — Guide
item.description: Hiroshima Castle, nicknamed the Carp Castle, was originally built in the 1590s by the warlord Mori Terumoto as the seat of his domain, a striking black-walled keep on the delta plain. The original survived until 1945, when it was destroyed by the atomic bomb; the present five-storey keep is a faithful concrete reconstruction of 1958, its dark timber-look exterior rising from a broad moat and stone base. Inside is a well-presented museum of the castle’s history and samurai culture, and the top floor gives a view over the rebuilt city.

item.title: Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum: Bearing Witness — Guide
item.description: The Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum, at the southern end of the Peace Park, is one of the most important and affecting museums in the world. Extensively renewed in 2019, it presents the atomic bombing of 6 August 1945 not through statistics but through the human beings who lived and died that day: a child’s scorched tricycle, a stopped watch, tattered school uniforms, photographs of the ruined city and the personal testimonies of survivors, the hibakusha.

item.title: Iwakuni Castle: Hilltop Keep Above the Nishiki — Guide
item.description: Iwakuni Castle crowns the summit of Mount Yokoyama, high above the Nishiki River and the famous Kintaikyo Bridge in eastern Yamaguchi. Originally built in the early seventeenth century by the Kikkawa lords, it was dismantled soon after under the shogunate’s one-castle-per-domain rule and rebuilt in the twentieth century as the handsome white keep seen today. A cable car climbs the mountain in a few minutes, and from the top the reward is a sweeping panorama: the five arches of the Kintaikyo directly below, the town spreading along the river, and the islands of the Seto Inland Sea beyond.

item.title: Karatsu Castle: The Castle by the Sea — Guide
item.description: Karatsu Castle stands on a low hill above the sea where the Matsuura River flows into Karatsu Bay, its white walls and tiled roofs looking especially graceful against the water — earning it the nickname ‘Maizuru-jo’ (dancing crane castle) and, for the way it seems to float above the coast, the ‘floating castle’. Though the present keep is a modern reconstruction, its hilltop setting is superb: from the top there are sweeping views over the bay, the town, and the famous Niji-no-Matsubara, a two-hundred-year-old pine grove stretching several kilometres along the shore.

item.title: Kochi Castle: One of Japan's Original Keeps — Guide
item.description: Kochi Castle is one of Japan’s great treasures: one of just twelve castles nationwide to retain its original wooden keep, and the only one to also preserve its original main palace hall together with the keep. Built in the early Edo period by the Yamauchi lords who ruled the Tosa domain, it rises on a hill in the heart of Kochi city, its white tower reached through a series of gates, walls and stone ramparts that survive largely intact.

item.title: Kofukuji Temple — Guide
item.description: Kofukuji, in the Teramachi temple district of central Nagasaki, is the oldest Chinese Ōbaku Zen temple in Japan, founded in 1620 by the city’s Chinese community. It was here that the influential Chinese monk Ingen (Yinyuan) first taught after arriving in Japan in 1654, effectively making Kofukuji the birthplace of the Ōbaku school of Zen in Japan — a sect that would go on to shape Japanese Buddhism, art and even cuisine.

item.title: Kumamoto Castle — Guide
item.description: Kumamoto Castle, rising on a hill in the heart of the city, is one of Japan’s three great castles and among the country’s most magnificent fortresses. Built in the early seventeenth century by the master castle-builder Katō Kiyomasa, it is famous for its imposing black-and-white keep and, above all, its formidable defensive stonework — steeply curving ‘musha-gaeshi’ walls that sweep up almost vertically to repel attackers, considered some of the finest castle masonry in Japan.

item.title: Kumamoto Prefectural Museum — Guide
item.description: The Kumamoto Prefectural Museum, near Suizenji Garden, is a broad, family-friendly museum covering the natural history, geology, archaeology and history of Kumamoto prefecture. Its exhibits range across the region’s dynamic natural environment — shaped by the great Aso volcano — its wildlife and fossils, and its human history from ancient times through the samurai era, presented in an accessible, engaging way. A popular highlight is its planetarium, projecting the night sky and astronomy shows, and there are hands-on and interactive displays that make it especially good for children.

item.title: Marugame Castle: Towering Stone Walls — Guide
item.description: Marugame Castle is one of Japan’s twelve castles to retain its original wooden keep, and though the keep itself is one of the smallest, the castle is famous for something else: its stone walls. Rising in tiers up the hill of Kameyama, the ramparts are among the tallest and most beautifully curved in Japan, sweeping upward in graceful concave lines to a total height of around 60 metres — a masterpiece of Edo-period stone-fitting.

item.title: Matsuyama Castle: Hilltop Original Keep — Guide
item.description: Matsuyama Castle stands on Mount Katsuyama in the very centre of the city, one of just twelve Japanese castles to keep its original Edo-period wooden keep. It is among the finest of them all: a complete hilltop complex of interconnected keeps, turrets and gates, built for defence with clever twisting approaches, and beautifully preserved. A ropeway or chairlift carries you up the hill (or you can walk), and from the top the reward is a magnificent 360-degree panorama over Matsuyama to the islands of the Seto Inland Sea.

item.title: Miyazaki Prefectural Museum — Guide
item.description: The Miyazaki Prefectural Museum of Nature and History, set in the green surroundings of Miyazaki Jingu shrine’s park in the city, is an excellent free introduction to the prefecture. Its wide-ranging exhibits cover Miyazaki’s natural environment — from its subtropical coast to its mountains and wildlife — as well as its rich archaeology and history, including material connected to the ancient burial mounds of Saitobaru and the region’s deep mythological heritage.

item.title: Nagasaki Atomic Bomb Museum — Guide
item.description: The Nagasaki Atomic Bomb Museum, beside the Peace Park, tells the story of the atomic bombing of the city on 9 August 1945 and its aftermath. Through harrowing photographs, scorched and melted artefacts — a stopped clock frozen at 11:02, twisted metal, everyday objects deformed by the heat — as well as survivor (hibakusha) testimony, models and film, it conveys both the scale of the destruction and the intensely human tragedy of the day.

item.title: Nagasaki Museum of History and Culture — Guide
item.description: The Nagasaki Museum of History and Culture, in the Tateyama district, is devoted to the city’s remarkable history as Japan’s principal gateway for overseas trade and cultural exchange during its centuries of isolation. Its well-designed exhibits explore how goods, people, religions and ideas from China, the Netherlands and beyond flowed through Nagasaki, shaping a uniquely cosmopolitan local culture — from imported art and crafts to the fusion food and festivals still seen today.

item.title: Nagasaki Peace Park — Guide
item.description: Nagasaki Peace Park, laid out on a hill near the hypocentre of the atomic bomb dropped on 9 August 1945, is the city’s foremost place of remembrance and its prayer for a world without nuclear weapons. At its heart stands the monumental Peace Statue, a ten-metre bronze figure whose raised right hand points to the threat of nuclear weapons and whose outstretched left hand symbolises peace. Nearby, the Fountain of Peace remembers victims who died desperate for water, and monuments donated by countries around the world line the grounds.

item.title: Nakatsu Castle — Guide
item.description: Nakatsu Castle, in the coastal town of Nakatsu in northern Oita, is a handsome reconstructed castle counted among Japan’s notable ‘water castles’, built where the river meets the sea. It was founded in the late sixteenth century by Kuroda Kanbei (Yoshitaka), one of the most brilliant strategists of Japan’s warring-states era, and later held by the Okudaira clan. The elegant black keep, rebuilt in the twentieth century, houses a museum of samurai armour, weapons and local history, and its stone walls — among the oldest surviving parts — are admired by castle enthusiasts.

item.title: Okayama Castle: The Black Crow Castle — Guide
item.description: Okayama Castle is known as Ujo, the Crow Castle, for the striking black lacquered boards that clad its walls — a deliberate contrast to the white ‘White Heron’ castle at Himeji. Originally completed in 1597 by Ukita Hideie, it stood on the bank of the Asahi River, which served as its natural moat, until the keep was destroyed in a wartime air raid in 1945. The present keep is a 1966 reconstruction, extensively renewed in 2022, housing a well-presented museum of the castle and its lords, with a top-floor view over the river to Korakuen garden directly opposite.

item.title: Reigando Cave: Musashi Miyamoto's Retreat — Guide
item.description: Reigando, a mountain cave in the hills west of Kumamoto city, is famous as the retreat where the legendary swordsman and philosopher Miyamoto Musashi spent his final years and wrote his celebrated treatise on strategy and swordsmanship, ‘The Book of Five Rings’ (Go Rin no Sho), around 1643. Undefeated in over sixty duels, Musashi withdrew to this quiet cave to meditate and set down his life’s wisdom, and the atmospheric grotto — with a small shrine and statue inside — has drawn pilgrims and admirers ever since.

item.title: Saga Prefectural Museum and Art Museum — Guide
item.description: The Saga Prefectural Museum and the adjoining Saga Prefectural Art Museum, set together beside the greenery of Saga Castle park in the heart of the city, form the prefecture’s main cultural complex. The museum covers Saga’s natural history, archaeology and history — including material connected to the Yoshinogari ancient site, the prefecture’s important role in Japan’s modernisation, and its ceramics and culture — through well-presented exhibits. The art museum next door displays works by artists connected to Saga alongside changing exhibitions.

item.title: Saitobaru Burial Mounds — Guide
item.description: The Saitobaru area of central Miyazaki is home to one of the largest and most important concentrations of ancient burial mounds (kofun) in Japan, a vast archaeological park set among rolling grassland and woodland. Scattered across the site are more than 300 tombs built between the 3rd and 7th centuries for local rulers, ranging from small round mounds to enormous keyhole-shaped kofun over 100 metres long, now grassed-over green hills dotted across the landscape.

item.title: Sakamoto Ryoma Memorial Museum, Kochi — Guide
item.description: Sakamoto Ryoma is Kochi’s greatest hero: a low-ranking samurai from Tosa who became a visionary of the movement to overthrow the shogunate, broker alliances and open Japan to the modern world, only to be assassinated in Kyoto at just 31. This striking modern museum, perched on the headland above Katsurahama beach where his famous statue stands, tells his life and turbulent times through letters, artefacts and immersive displays, with dramatic ocean views from its galleries.

item.title: Shimonoseki and the Kanmon Strait — Guide
item.description: The Kanmon Strait is the narrow, fast-flowing channel that separates Honshu from Kyushu at Japan’s western end, with the port city of Shimonoseki on one side and Kitakyushu on the other, barely a kilometre apart. It has been a strategic waterway for centuries — the site of the decisive 1185 sea battle that ended the Genpei War, and later of the town’s opening to foreign trade. Today the strait is crossed by the soaring Kanmon Bridge, by rail and road tunnels, and remarkably by a pedestrian tunnel you can walk under the sea from one prefecture to another.

item.title: Siebold Memorial Museum — Guide
item.description: The Siebold Memorial Museum, in the Narutaki district where the physician once lived, honours Philipp Franz von Siebold, the German doctor who arrived at the Dutch trading post of Dejima in 1823 and became one of the most important figures in the exchange of knowledge between Japan and the West. At his private school Narutaki-juku he taught Western medicine and science to Japanese students, while himself studying and cataloguing Japanese plants, animals and culture, sending vast collections back to Europe that shaped Western understanding of Japan.

item.title: Tokyo National Museum — Guide
item.description: The Tokyo National Museum (Tokyo Kokuritsu Hakubutsukan), founded in 1872 and set in Ueno Park, is Japan’s oldest and largest museum, and home to the world’s most comprehensive collection of Japanese art and archaeology. Its vast holdings — over 110,000 items including scores of designated National Treasures and Important Cultural Properties — span the whole sweep of Japanese culture: samurai swords and armour, exquisite Buddhist sculpture, painted screens and scrolls, ceramics, lacquerware, ukiyo-e woodblock prints, kimono and textiles, and archaeological finds.

item.title: Urakami Cathedral — Guide
item.description: Urakami Cathedral, in the north of Nagasaki, is a red-brick Catholic church with a poignant history bound up with both the persecution of Christians and the atomic bomb. Built by local Catholics in the early twentieth century — descendants of the ‘hidden Christians’ who had secretly kept their faith through 250 years of brutal persecution — it was once the largest church in East Asia. On 9 August 1945 it stood just 500 metres from the hypocentre and was almost completely destroyed, killing those inside.

item.title: Uwajima Castle: A Small Original Keep — Guide
item.description: Uwajima Castle, in the southern port city of Uwajima, is one of Japan’s twelve castles to retain its original Edo-period wooden keep. Small and elegant rather than grand, its three-storey white tower crowns a wooded hill in the middle of the city, reached by a climb through stone walls and old gates among the trees. Built by the Date clan who ruled the domain, it survived the centuries intact and offers a genuine taste of a modest samurai-era castle, with views over Uwajima and its bay from the top.

item.title: Yashima: Flat-Topped Plateau and History — Guide
item.description: Yashima is a striking flat-topped lava plateau that rises steeply above the coast just east of Takamatsu, its level summit and sheer sides making it a local landmark. From the top, terraces and viewpoints command sweeping panoramas over Takamatsu, the island-dotted Seto Inland Sea, and the surrounding coast — especially beautiful at sunset. The plateau is steeped in history: it was the site of the Battle of Yashima in 1185, a famous clash of the Genpei War between the Minamoto and Taira clans, remembered in legend and place names.

item.title: Yoshinogari Historic Site: Ancient Japan — Guide
item.description: The Yoshinogari Historic Site is one of the most significant archaeological discoveries in Japan, a huge moated settlement from the Yayoi period (roughly 300 BC–300 AD) that flourished here around 2,000 years ago. Excavations revealed the largest such site in the country — a fortified village of encircling moats, wooden watchtowers, storehouses and burial mounds — offering an extraordinary glimpse of Japan’s rice-farming society before recorded history, and possibly linked to the legendary early kingdom described in ancient Chinese chronicles.

item.title: Chiba Castle Guide: Museum, Cherry Blossoms & Access
item.description: In the heart of Chiba City, Chiba Castle crowns the leafy Inohana hill where the powerful Chiba clan once ruled the region in the medieval era. The handsome white keep you see today is a modern reconstruction housing the Chiba City Folk Museum, which traces the clan’s history and local samurai culture. Surrounded by Inohana Park — one of the city’s best cherry-blossom spots — and close to the venerable Chiba Shrine, it makes an easy, pleasant half-day of history, greenery and city sightseeing right by central Chiba.

item.title: Himeyuri Peace Museum Guide: Access & What to Know
item.description: The Himeyuri Peace Memorial Museum in Itoman, in southern Okinawa, tells one of the most moving stories of the Battle of Okinawa (1945). The “Himeyuri” were a group of around 200 teenage schoolgirls and their teachers mobilised as a student nursing corps; most lost their lives in the final weeks of the battle. The museum and adjacent monument, built where many died, preserve their testimonies, photographs and belongings as a powerful plea for peace.

item.title: Imperial Palace Guide: East Gardens, Edo Castle Ruins & Tokyo's Green Heart
item.description: In the very centre of Tokyo, surrounded by the glass towers of Marunouchi and the rush of the financial district, lies a vast island of moats, stone walls, pine forests, and manicured gardens: the Tokyo Imperial Palace, official residence of the Emperor of Japan. This is the site of Edo Castle, once the largest fortress in the world and the seat of the Tokugawa shoguns who ruled Japan for 260 years.

item.title: Jidai Matsuri Guide: Kyoto's Festival of the Ages
item.description: Imagine over a thousand years of Japanese history marching past you in a single afternoon. That’s Jidai Matsuri, the “Festival of the Ages” — Kyoto’s grand historical-costume procession held every October 22. Some 2,000 participants in meticulously researched costumes representing every major era from the Heian period to the Meiji Restoration parade through the city in reverse chronological order, a living timeline of Japan’s emperors, samurai, nobles, and famous historical figures.

item.title: Odawara Castle & Hojo Festival Guide: What to See & Access
item.description: The castle town of Odawara, gateway to Hakone, was once the mighty stronghold of the Hojo clan who ruled much of eastern Japan until Toyotomi Hideyoshi’s famous siege in 1590. Today its handsomely reconstructed castle keep anchors a park of cherry trees and museums, and each spring the town celebrates its samurai past with the Hojo Godai Festival, when costumed warriors, princesses and musicians parade through the streets. Add a moat-side bloom of cherry blossoms, a hilltop view to the sea, and the town’s famous kamaboko fish cake, and Odawara makes a rewarding history stop on the way to Hakone.

item.title: Osaka Castle Guide: The Tower, Park & Best Times to Visit
item.description: Rising on its great stone base above a sea of green, Osaka Castle is the symbol of the city and its single most famous sight. The gleaming white-and-green keep, trimmed with golden tigers and crests, sits within a vast park ringed by massive stone walls and broad moats — a monument to Toyotomi Hideyoshi, the warlord who unified Japan and built his power base here in the 16th century. Today the keep houses a modern museum, the top floor offers sweeping city views, and the surrounding park is one of Osaka’s best spots for cherry and plum blossom.

item.title: Ryukyu Gusuku Guide: Zakimi Castle & UNESCO Ruins
item.description: Long before Shuri unified the islands, Okinawa was dotted with gusuku — the fortified castles of rival Ryukyu lords. Several of their dramatic ruins, prized for their flowing, beautifully engineered curved limestone walls, are inscribed together as UNESCO World Heritage (“Gusuku Sites and Related Properties of the Kingdom of Ryukyu”). Zakimi Castle in Yomitan is among the most accessible and best preserved, its ramparts open to walk and offering views to the sea.

item.title: Shuri Castle Guide: Tickets, Reconstruction & Access (Naha)
item.description: Shuri Castle (Shurijō) was the political and ceremonial heart of the Ryukyu Kingdom for some 450 years, and remains Okinawa’s most important historic site. With its distinctive vermilion halls, Chinese- and Japanese-influenced architecture, and hilltop views over Naha, it is a UNESCO World Heritage component (“Gusuku Sites and Related Properties of the Kingdom of Ryukyu”). A devastating fire in October 2019 destroyed the main hall (Seiden) and several structures; the castle is now in the midst of a multi-year reconstruction, which has itself become a fascinating thing to witness.

item.title: Lake Biwa Complete Guide: Japan's Ancient Inland Sea
item.description: Lake Biwa is not simply a large lake. At 670 square kilometres, it is Japan’s largest body of freshwater, and its shores have been inhabited, crossed, worshipped, and fought over for at least fourteen centuries. The lake predates the oldest surviving structures on its banks; its name derives from the biwa lute, whose shape the water body loosely resembles when viewed from the surrounding mountains. For overseas visitors who know Shiga at all, they tend to know it as the prefecture that contains Lake Biwa — and they are right to think of the lake first, because everything in Shiga orbits around it.

item.title: Okinawa Sightseeing Guide: Shuri Castle, Ryukyu Heritage & Hidden Spots
item.description: Okinawa’s history is unlike anywhere else in Japan. For 450 years (1429–1879) it was the independent Ryukyu Kingdom — a maritime trading nation with its own language, religion, architecture, and performing arts. The Ryukyuan legacy is everywhere: in the bright red lacquer of its castles (gusuku), the sound of the sanshin (three-stringed lute), and a cuisine built on tropical ingredients rather than the rice and soy of mainland Japan. 1.

item.title: Hokkaido Mystery Guide: Escape Rooms, Goryokaku's Last Republic & Ainu Secrets
item.description: Hokkaido’s mysteries operate at an unusual intersection of the very recent (150 years of recorded colonial history) and the very ancient (10,000+ years of Ainu culture that the colonisation systematically attempted to erase). The island’s short institutional history means the historical record is remarkably complete — Enomoto Takeaki’s Republic of Ezo lasted less than a year and is documented in extraordinary detail — while the Ainu cultural codes embedded in Hokkaido’s landscape names have only recently begun to be properly interpreted.
